utterance: Hi Daniel, I’m sorry your back is giving you trouble. Tell me what happened when this started and how the pain has changed since.
reply: It happened on Saturday when I was lifting a big pot plant in the garden and felt a twinge, and then I woke up Sunday and could barely get out of bed, so it has been three days now. The pain is low down on the left side of my back and sometimes goes into my left buttock, and it gets worse when I bend or get out of a chair or by the evening, though it feels a bit better lying still with a heat pack. I have worked from home the last two days mostly lying on the couch with my laptop, and I can walk around slowly.

utterance:
Your examination shows tenderness and muscle spasm on the left, but normal strength, feeling and reflexes in both legs, without signs of a trapped nerve. This fits an acute mechanical back strain. I can’t tell exactly which muscle, joint or disc is sore, but we don't need a scan to manage this safely now. MRIs often show disc bulges in people without pain; early scans don't improve recovery in this situation and can lead to unnecessary worry or treatment. We would reconsider imaging if warning signs develop or you aren't recovering as expected.

Before choosing pain relief: do you take any medicines or supplements, and have you had any medicine reactions apart from tramadol? Have you ever had a stomach ulcer or bleeding, kidney or heart disease, or asthma triggered by aspirin or anti-inflammatory medicines such as ibuprofen?
reply: I don't have any regular medicines, I have no history of stomach ulcers, my kidneys are fine as far as I know, and I don't have asthma.

utterance:
For the next few days you can try ibuprofen, two 200 mg tablets with food up to three times a day when needed, no more than six tablets in 24 hours. Use the lowest amount that helps, and stop as the pain settles. Don't combine it with other anti-inflammatory medicines such as naproxen or diclofenac, or take extra ibuprofen under another brand. Stop it and seek help for severe stomach pain, black stools, vomiting blood, wheezing or reduced urine; avoid it if dehydrated. Paracetamol alone often doesn't help this kind of pain, so there's no need to keep taking it if it's not helping. Strong opioid painkillers aren't recommended here.

Movement is part of recovery: take short, frequent walks and gently increase normal activities rather than staying on the couch or in bed. Some discomfort with movement doesn't mean you're damaging your back. For now avoid heavy lifting and repeated twisting, then build back gradually. A wrapped heat pack for 15–20 minutes can help; don't sleep on it. At work, change positions regularly, take short walking breaks, and use a desk rather than working lying on the couch. Temporary shorter hours or modified duties are reasonable, and I can provide a certificate if needed. Most episodes improve substantially within a couple of weeks, although settling fully can take four to six weeks.
reply: I can ask for a certificate if I need one for work, but I was really hoping we could just do the scan so I can know for sure what is going on.

utterance:
I hear that you want certainty, especially after reading about surgery. A scan can show the shape of the discs but usually can't tell us which part is causing this kind of pain. Your normal nerve examination and absence of warning symptoms make a serious problem unlikely, so an MRI now is more likely to confuse things than help. This isn't dismissing the pain—it can be very painful even without serious damage. Let's actively treat it and check your progress rather than simply leave it.

I'd like to review you in a week, sooner if you're getting worse or the pain isn't manageable. If you're not clearly improving over the next couple of weeks, we can reassess and arrange physiotherapy for guided activity and exercise. If symptoms persist around four to six weeks, we'll review again whether imaging or a specialist would change treatment.

Go straight to an emergency department if you develop trouble passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness around your genitals or bottom, or new or worsening leg weakness. Seek urgent same-day care for fever or feeling very unwell with back pain, or severe unrelenting pain, particularly at rest or overnight. Please also let me know about new leg pain or numbness, or unexpected weight loss.

How does that plan sound, and is there anything that would make it difficult to follow?
reply: I will try the ibuprofen and get off the couch to do some walking, but I am still worried that missing the scan might mean we are overlooking something serious.

utterance: That's understandable. Nothing in today's history or examination points to cancer, infection, fracture or dangerous nerve pressure. No assessment gives a 100% guarantee, but the safest evidence-based approach here is treatment, a planned review and clear instructions about changes that need urgent attention—not a routine scan now. If anything changes, we'll reassess rather than stick to today's conclusion. Please book that review for next week so we can check you're improving. Just to check I've explained clearly, which changes would make you seek emergency help?
reply: Trouble passing urine, loss of bladder or bowel control, numbness around my bottom, or new leg weakness.

awards.label: Defensible diagnosis: Lumbar muscle strain
Can't-miss diagnosis considered: Cauda equina syndrome

utterance: Exactly—seek emergency help straight away for those changes. Start with short walks and the short course of pain relief, and we'll review you next week. Please contact us earlier if you're worsening or can't manage at home.
